Spikedace (Meda fulgida) embryos begin development within demersal, adhesive eggs that measure approximately 1.5 millimeters in diameter. From the estimated egg volume, the calculated wet weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams], reflecting the modest energetic reserves packaged within each ovum prior to fertilization. Following eclosion, these prolarvae remain in a lecithotrophic state, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding upon mouth opening and yolk-sac resorption. The larval period is characterized by rapid somatic growth within the thermally stable spring and early summer flows of the upper Gila River basin. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the species exhibits a total lifespan of approximately 1,460 days [am = approximately 1,460 days], a value that corresponds to about four years and aligns well with mark-recapture estimates from wild populations in Aravaipa Creek. This comparatively short lifespan, typical of many small-bodied cyprinids, imposes strong selective pressure for early maturation and efficient allocation of resources toward reproductive output during the limited adult window.

Sexual maturation in Spikedace occurs at a relatively modest body size, marking the transition from the juvenile growth phase into reproductive adulthood. The total length at puberty has been recorded at 4.56 centimeters [Lp = 4.56 centimeters], a metric derived from standard length measurements of approximately 3.9 centimeters. At this size, individuals have typically completed the larval-juvenile transformation and entered the immature post-metamorphic stage, with gonadal recrudescence initiating under the influence of rising spring water temperatures and photoperiod cues. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, estimated from the length-weight relationship for this species, is approximately 0.76 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.76 grams], indicating that individuals allocate substantial somatic growth toward achieving a minimum body condition before the onset of gametogenesis. This size threshold is relatively low compared to other members of the family Leuciscidae occupying similar desert stream habitats, suggesting an adaptive strategy that prioritizes early reproduction in an environment characterized by unpredictable flow regimes and intermittent habitat availability. Field surveys indicate that most individuals reach this developmental milestone during their first year of life, provided adequate thermal and trophic conditions prevail.

Fully grown Spikedace achieve a maximum recorded body size that represents the ultimate total length attainable under natural conditions. The ultimate total length for this species has been documented at 9.1 centimeters [Li = 9.1 centimeters], corresponding to a large, reproductively active adult in excellent condition. At this asymptotic size, individuals have typically completed allometric shifts in body plan associated with the larval-juvenile transition and have entered the sexually mature adult stage. The predicted wet weight for an individual of this ultimate length, derived from the species-specific length-weight conversion formula, is approximately 6.37 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.37 grams], reflecting the substantial mass gain achieved during the post-pubertal growth interval. Comparisons with sympatric leuciscids such as the loach minnow (Rhinichthys cobitis) reveal that Spikedace attains a comparable maximum size, consistent with the convergent life-history strategies observed among small-bodied desert fishes adapted to similarly constrained thermal and hydrologic regimes. These maximum dimensions are rarely observed in heavily fragmented habitats where premature mortality from predation or flow intermittency truncates the size distribution.

Reproductive output in Spikedace has been quantified through direct observation of spawning events under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], individuals measuring 92 millimeters in standard length and 108 millimeters in total length produce an average of approximately 1,749 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,749 eggs per spawning event]. Given that females typically complete a single spawning pulse each year [F_R_i = single spawning pulse each year] under these same thermal conditions, the annual reproductive output is substantial for a fish of this body size. The eggs, once fertilized through broadcast spawning over gravel substrates, develop as demersal incubating eggs that adhere firmly to the substrate until eclosion. This reproductive strategy, characterized by a single, high-fecundity annual event, contrasts with the multiple-clutch pattern observed in some other small desert cyprinids and likely reflects an adaptation to the narrow temporal window of favorable spring flows in the species' native range. The high fecundity per event compensates for the relatively short lifespan and provides a demographic buffer against years of poor recruitment.

The early life stages of Spikedace are particularly vulnerable to environmental variation, and the transition from the yolk-dependent embryo to the exogenously feeding pelagic larva represents a critical bottleneck in the species' life cycle. Following eclosion, the prolarvae, weighing just 1.8 milligrams [Wwb = 1.8 milligrams] at emergence, must quickly locate and capture suitable microzooplankton prey to sustain the rapid growth rates necessary for survival. Field observations indicate that the onset of exogenous feeding coincides with swim bladder inflation and retinal differentiation, enabling active pursuit of prey items in the water column. The exotrophic transition is completed within the first few days post-hatching, after which the free-swimming larvae enter a planktonic phase characterized by high mortality rates from both starvation and predation. In contrast, the later juvenile stage, once individuals have reached the fingerling size class, is marked by considerably higher survivorship and the progressive accumulation of body mass toward the pubertal threshold of 0.76 grams [Wwp = 0.76 grams]. The species' life-history strategy thus balances a brief, high-risk larval period against a single, high-fecundity reproductive event to maintain population persistence in the variable desert stream environment.
